title: The night hackers turned Europe’s supermarkets into ovens
dek: Over a few weeks this autumn, someone reached through the internet and told supermarket freezers in seven countries to heat up. Nobody has asked for a single euro.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: Refrigerated display cases in a grocery store.
body: **Update, 16 November:** On 9 November, France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps carried out the 11–12 October attacks on French supermarkets, and the Paris prosecutor’s office requested international arrest warrants for the leader of an IRGC-linked cyber unit and two deputies. Investigators cited the attackers’ use of Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices in Iran. France’s accusation covers the October attacks in France, not the 2 November wave in other countries. The story below was published on 4 November, before the accusation.

It happened at 2 a.m., the hour when a supermarket is at its most defenceless. Shelves stocked. Lights low. Staff gone home. At an ICA franchise store in Stockholm, the freezers began to heat up, and nobody was there to see it.
Hours passed before anyone noticed. By then the damage was done. “Everything is destroyed,” the store’s sales manager, Engla Ingwall, told Reuters.

Nobody broke a window. Nobody forced a lock. Somebody, somewhere, simply reached through the internet and told the freezers to get hot. In some European stores, the units were pushed as high as 50 degrees Celsius. That’s 122 Fahrenheit: a heatwave inside a metal box.
Over about four weeks this autumn, the same trick has hit supermarkets in seven countries. And the strangest part isn’t the heat. It’s that, so far, nobody has asked for a single euro.
## The story at a glance

- **11–12 October:** Hundreds of French supermarkets hit overnight. Temperatures up to 50°C, spoiled food, and fires reported by police.
- **2 November:** Fridges and freezers at more than 100 shops hit across Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Ireland and Estonia.
- **No ransom demand reported.** No group has claimed responsibility.
- **Two criminal investigations:** one in Paris, one in Belgium.
## A Monday morning in France

France went first. Overnight between 11 and 12 October, the cooling systems at hundreds of stores run by Intermarché, Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix and others were forced into defrost mode and, reportedly, kept there. One account puts the number of Les Mousquetaires stores (the group behind Intermarché) at 300 or more. Other counts are lower, and the figures differ from report to report.
Then the staff arrived.

Picture opening a supermarket and finding empty chiller cabinets and bins full of what used to be dinner. At one Intermarché store, about €50,000 of frozen food was reportedly lost. Coopérative U’s chief executive said that at a big store, losses could reach about €200,000. The owner of Intermarché told CNBC it expected damages of several million euros.
The Paris prosecutor opened an investigation. Coopérative U’s boss called the attack “unprecedented.” Few people disagreed.
## The embarrassingly simple part

Here’s where the story gets uncomfortable. According to reports, the attackers didn’t need exotic tricks. Security researchers found thousands of refrigeration controllers made by the Danish company Danfoss that could be reached from the internet, many of them in France, and searchable with tools that list internet-connected devices. Remote access is handy for a repair crew. It’s also a doorbell that anyone can ring.
Danfoss said the devices involved were older ones running outdated firmware, and that it had urged customers to update them. Known weaknesses in these controllers date back to 2023, and fixes exist.

Awais Rashid, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Bristol, told Al Jazeera the same story from another angle. Many refrigeration systems are managed remotely by third parties, he said. They sit where the internet can reach them, several controllers have known vulnerabilities, and some still have easily guessable passwords.
It’s less like picking a lock and more like finding a door nobody ever shut, then discovering there’s a search engine that lists open doors.
One report adds a nasty detail: some defrost cycles were reportedly stretched to eight hours, which would delay temperature alarms. Treat that one as a claim, not a finding.
## No ransom. No thieves. So why?

This is the part that doesn’t fit the usual cybercrime playbook. Normally the story ends with a ransom demand, or a pile of stolen customer data. Not here. No ransom demand has been reported, and there’s no evidence of data theft.

The pattern has shown up before. In the US, freezers at the commissary on Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona, went into defrost mode in August, spoiling frozen food, and Naval Station Newport in Rhode Island was among the other affected bases. Reuters reported that the Pentagon was treating the incidents as a suspected hack.
So what’s the point of cooking a freezer full of fish fingers?

Nobody knows for sure. Europe’s agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, called the attacks a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence.” Rashid warned that the attacks risk undermining trust in infrastructure people rely on every day.
## The second wave
If anyone hoped France was a one-off, 2 November ended that hope.

The pattern jumped borders. In Belgium and Luxembourg, Delhaize and Colruyt reported an overnight “IT incident.” Sabcobel, the refrigeration company that runs Delhaize’s systems, said units had been switched to defrost mode in a cyberattack. Carrefour said about 15 of its roughly 700 Belgian stores were affected. In Sweden, ICA and Coop reported trouble, and an ICA store manager said fridge and freezer settings had been changed to 50°C and could not be modified while staff threw away stock. In Ireland, wholesaler Musgrave said 13 SuperValu stores were affected. One IKEA site in Mons, Belgium, was hit too.

And the cost wasn’t only corporate. A Belgian butcher’s shop in Hove, south of Antwerp, saw its fridges pushed to 18°C, ruining meat worth around €15,000. For a small business, that’s a bad month, from one night.
Belgian prosecutors opened a criminal investigation.
## Who is behind it?

When this story was published, nobody had said, and nobody had claimed it. There was plenty of speculation. European intelligence officials have warned that Russia is escalating a shadow war on the continent, and cyberattacks are among its tools. But warnings about a general threat aren’t evidence about this attack, so we left the name blank until investigators filled it in. (See the update at the top.)

What officials are saying out loud is more worrying than any single culprit. On 3 November, Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre said an AI-powered ransomware attack on the country’s critical infrastructure is highly likely by 2028. And the UK has launched a “Be Ready” campaign, asking households to keep three days of supplies, including food that needs no cooking, bottled water and cash.
## Why a fridge?
Because that’s the point.

A hacked bank is scary but abstract. A hacked fridge is something you can smell. It turns a quiet piece of infrastructure into a headline, and it chips away at a small thing we all rely on without thinking: the quiet assumption that the milk will be cold.

Rashid made a point worth remembering. A lot of our digital infrastructure operates safely every day, he said, because good security practices enable that. The problem is that attackers only need the forgotten corners, the dull gadget on the wall that nobody has looked at in ten years.
## If you run a shop, a café or a warehouse
This section is our advice, not the investigators’. But it follows directly from what went wrong.

- **Ask your installer which devices are online,** and who can log in to them.
- **Change default or simple passwords** on anything you control.
- **Check whether your controllers are still supported.** Old ones stop getting fixes.
- **Buy a cheap thermometer with its own alarm,** not connected to your network.
- **Write down who you’ll call at 2 a.m.,** and where you’ll move the stock.
If you’re just a shopper: no need to panic. So far the damage has mostly been financial, in spoiled stock and clean-up costs for the shops that were hit.

title: Singapore’s hottest tech stocks just lost about a quarter of their value in a month
dek: Singapore’s tech stocks just had their worst month of 2026: the sector index lost 17.3% in October, and today’s Asia-wide selloff is keeping the pressure on.
author: Ethan Koh
caption: Share prices on a trading screen.
body: ## October was ugly, and tech took the worst of it

The Straits Times Index lost 5.2% in October on a total-return basis. Tech did far worse. The sector index fell 17.3%, the worst of any sector that month. S-REITs, by comparison, barely flinched at 1.4%.
The chip and electronics names got hammered:

- AEM: down 24% for the month, still up 335% for the year
- UMS Integration: down 26%, still up 80%
- Frencken: down 23%, still up 47%
- PC Partner: down 22%, still up 211%
These stocks ran so hard in 2026 that even a drop like that leaves them well ahead.
## It started in America

Investors on Wall Street have been getting nervous about how much money is going into AI and when it will actually pay off. Alphabet dropped 12.6% in a single session late last month, and by Oct 30 Singapore’s chip-linked stocks were feeling it. AEM fell 8.6% that day. The STI only slipped 0.4% to 5,376.74, because the banks and the rest of the index cushioned the blow.

Then came this week’s US midterms. Democrats won big, and the market immediately started worrying about tighter rules for AI. Several winning candidates have promised to curb data centre construction. The fear is that fewer data centres means less demand for the chips and equipment behind them. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% overnight, its worst day since April 2025.

Asia caught the fallout this morning. Seoul was down almost 9% at one point, Taipei about 8% and Tokyo 7%. Singapore was off more than 1% in early trading, so we got off lighter than most. That’s not the same as being immune.
## Big money is leaving, small investors are staying

Institutions pulled a net S$1.55 billion out of Singapore stocks in October. Retail investors went the other way and bought S$1.65 billion, which takes their net buying to S$5.9 billion for the first ten months of the year.
After a run like AEM’s, big funds taking profits isn’t a shock. Whether retail investors are right to buy the dip is a different question, and nobody can answer it yet.
## So is this a crash?

Not on the business numbers so far. Electronics output is up 24.6% in the first nine months of the year, and manufacturing is up 9.8%. The factories are busy. What changed is how much investors are willing to pay for the stocks.

Three things to watch from here: the third-quarter earnings updates due this month, the US debate over AI regulation, and interest rates. If the results hold up, October may look like a reset after a huge run. If they don’t, it may have been the warm-up.
This is general information, not financial advice.
## Sources

- [SGX October market report, via Tiger Brokers](https://www.itiger.com/news/1179570946)
- [Singapore stocks slip as tech sell-off weighs on STI, BusinessToday](https://www.businesstoday.com.my/2026/10/31/singapore-stocks-slip-0-4-as-tech-sell-off-banking-losses-weigh-on-sti/)

title: Meet the coworker with no face
dek: A few years ago, “AI employee” sounded like a pitch from a sci-fi movie. Today it’s a line on the org chart.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: A robot at a laptop.
body: Take McKinsey. CEO Bob Sternfels said in January that the firm had added 25,000 AI agents, which it treats as digital employees, to a human workforce of about 40,000. Do the math and that’s roughly five software workers for every eight people on the payroll. And McKinsey isn’t a factory. It’s a firm that sells human judgment for a living.

This is a look at what AI employees actually are, where companies are putting them to work, why the results are still hard to prove, and what the rise of the AI workforce means for your career. If you’ve wondered whether this is hype or the real thing, the honest answer is a bit of both.
## One firm, 25,000 digital workers

Read that McKinsey number again. Sternfels has said the goal is for every one of the firm’s 40,000 people to have an AI agent working alongside them. That isn’t a pilot project in a corner of the business. It’s a plan for how the whole company runs.

McKinsey is the headline case, but it isn’t alone. Large companies in banking, retail, software and consulting are all trying versions of the same idea, and they’re no longer calling it an experiment. They call it hiring.
## What is an AI employee, and how is it different from a chatbot?

The old picture of workplace AI was a chatbot waiting for someone to type a question. AI employees, also called AI agents or digital workers, are different. Companies describe them as digital coworkers that act on their own, with their own identities, access permissions and responsibilities. You give one a goal, and it works through the tools it’s been given to get there: reading an inbox, updating a customer record, drafting a follow-up, flagging a problem for a human.
That’s basically what a new hire gets on day one.
## They get logins, just like you

The comparison to a human hire goes further than you’d expect. Companies are treating the first week of an AI agent like an onboarding. The advice floating around HR and IT teams is to give an agent clear guidelines, a defined role, limits on what it can touch, and someone to report to, the same as you would for a person.

There’s a practical reason. An agent with the wrong access can do real damage fast, just like a new employee who can see every file on the server. So the boring parts of employment, like permissions, oversight and accountability, are being rebuilt for software.
It also raises a question nobody has a good answer to yet. Somewhere right now, a manager is probably wondering who does the AI’s performance review.
## Why companies want AI employees in the first place

The pitch is simple, and it’s the same one every new technology makes. An AI agent works around the clock, doesn’t need a notice period, and can be copied. If a company needs ten more people for a busy season, hiring and training them takes months. Spinning up ten more agents can take an afternoon.
That’s the appeal for a finance chief. For a manager, the pitch is different: the boring part of the job, the part everyone keeps putting off, gets done without anyone having to ask.
Both pitches have some truth in them. Neither tells you what an agent does when something unusual happens, and that’s usually where the trouble starts.
## Where AI agents are actually working
Sales and marketing, mostly. One report on how teams are “hiring” AI employees put sales and marketing at the top of the list, at 26.1%, with customer support and operations close behind.

It makes sense when you look at the work. These jobs are full of repeated tasks: qualifying leads, sending follow-up emails, answering the same ten support questions, updating the same spreadsheet. Software never gets bored of any of that.
Typical jobs handed to AI agents right now include:

- Sorting and replying to routine customer support tickets
- Drafting and sending sales follow-ups
- Pulling reports and cleaning up data for operations teams
- Scheduling, reminders and other admin
## The hiring wave is just starting

The wave is still building. More than half of talent leaders at big companies said they planned to hire AI agents in 2026. That’s a striking thing to say about a category that barely existed in most job descriptions three years ago.
## The part nobody puts in the press release

Here’s where it gets awkward. Almost every large company is using AI in some form, but few can prove it’s paying off. Adoption is close to universal at the enterprise level, yet measurable returns are still rare. Plenty of businesses bought the shiny new teammate and aren’t sure what it’s actually delivering.
That gap between “we use AI” and “AI makes us money” is one of the biggest open questions in business right now. Until it closes, every AI workforce announcement deserves a second look.
## The squeeze on entry-level jobs

The people side is rougher. Stanford researchers tracking payroll data found that workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed jobs saw employment fall about 11% between late 2022 and June 2026, while employment in the least-exposed jobs grew about 10%. Their headline measure: young workers in the most exposed fields now hold about 19% fewer jobs than they would have if they’d kept pace with their less-exposed peers. Experienced workers in the same fields show no comparable gap.
The job postings tell a similar story. One analysis found that about 71% of AI-related openings at S&P 500 companies are senior roles, and only about 13% are open to junior candidates.
That’s a real problem, and it goes beyond fairness. Entry-level jobs are where people learn the work. If software takes the easy tasks, how does anyone become a senior person in ten years?
## What AI employees still can’t do

Agents are good at following a pattern. They struggle when the pattern breaks. Think of a customer who’s furious about something that isn’t covered in any policy, a client whose real problem isn’t the one written on the ticket, or a decision where two reasonable rules point in opposite directions. Those are the moments people realise a human is needed, and they’re exactly the moments an agent is most likely to get something wrong with total confidence.

There’s also the matter of context. A good employee knows the unwritten rules: which client is touchy, which deadline is real, which manager says yes but means no. An agent only knows what it has been told.
## Who’s responsible when an AI employee gets it wrong?

If an agent sends the wrong email, approves the wrong refund or shares a file with the wrong person, who answers for it? Not the software. The responsibility lands on a human, usually whoever set the agent up or the manager it reports to.

That’s why companies are building oversight into these roles from day one, with clear limits on what an agent can do alone and a person who signs off on the rest. It’s also why the people who will be most valuable in this new setup are the ones who can supervise: spot a mistake quickly and know when to step in.
## What to watch next

Three things will tell us whether this is a lasting change or another hype cycle. First, whether companies can finally show real returns from their AI spending. Second, whether entry-level hiring recovers or keeps shrinking. Third, whether the idea of managing a team that’s half human and half software becomes a normal job, or stays a headline.
## So are humans out?

Not quite. After a long stretch of cautious hiring, several of America’s biggest employers are adding people again, and they say human involvement is still essential. The work is shifting more than it’s disappearing. Instead of doing every task yourself, you’ll be the one deciding what the AI should do, checking its work and catching what it gets wrong.
McKinsey’s own numbers point the same way. The firm is adding agents, but it is also still employing tens of thousands of people.
## Sources

- [McKinsey’s 25,000 AI agents: augmentation, not replacement, DEV Community](https://dev.to/derivinate/mckinseys-25000-ai-agents-augmentation-not-replacement-42nb)
- [Canaries in the Coal Mine, August 2026 update, Stanford Digital Economy Lab](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/news/canariesaug26/)
- [Stanford warns AI is reshaping the job market, Quartz](https://qz.com/stanford-warns-ai-reshaping-the-job-market-gen-z)

title: Jensen Huang affair: Nvidia CEO faces board probe over Alice Huang, Megaspeed and spy claims as Nvidia stock takes a hit
dek: On Sunday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, and the company’s board responded by launching an independent investigation into reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: An Nvidia office building.
body: **Update, 13 November:** Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive and as a director on 12 November (US time), and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The story below was published on 9 November, before his resignation.

The reporting points to Alice Huang, an executive tied to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer that U.S. authorities were already eyeing over AI chip exports. By Monday, November 9, 2026, Nvidia stock was sliding roughly 4% to 6% in premarket trading, a jolt for a company valued near $4.5 trillion.

Why does a private lapse become a market event? Because Nvidia is the engine room of the global AI boom, and Washington is in the middle of deciding how tightly to leash the flow of its best chips toward China. A founder under board scrutiny, with a congressional briefing already requested, hands investors a risk they have never had to price: what happens to Nvidia if Huang is not the one steering?

A word on sourcing before we dig in. Everything here comes from published reporting and company statements. The intelligence claims rest largely on anonymous U.S. officials, and none have been publicly proven.
## Key takeaways

- Huang told employees he was “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues.
- The board put independent directors and outside counsel in charge of the probe, while saying it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.
- U.S. intelligence reportedly concluded that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather information on Huang. Those are reported assessments, not courtroom findings.
- Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and says official inspections turned up no violations.
- Nvidia shares have shed about 13% since October 28, the last close before The New York Times’ first spy report, per Yahoo Finance.
- Huang stays on as CEO for now, and President Trump says he should.
## Jensen Huang’s apology memo and admission

Huang’s memo, sent to staff on Sunday, November 8, opens with a blunt apology. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote, adding that his actions hurt her and their children. He took full responsibility, pledged to cooperate with the board’s investigation, and closed with a line that read as both plea and promise: leading Nvidia is “the privilege of my life.”
### What the memo did and did not say

Notably, the memo kept names out of it. CNBC reports that Huang mentioned neither Megaspeed nor Alice Huang, though he did refer to the board’s inquiry into the national security concerns raised in news reports.

The admission also marks a sharp turn. Nvidia had earlier described Huang’s contacts with Alice Huang as ordinary customer interactions, with no sensitive trade secrets or national security information shared. According to The Hill, a company spokesperson first waved off the relationship report before the memo landed.
### The board’s statement
On Sunday afternoon, the board stepped in. Its statement said it was acting “in light of recent reporting” that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The shape of the probe:

- A committee of independent directors leads the work, backed by outside independent counsel.
- The board says it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but promises to examine all available information.
- No deadline and no committee roster have been made public.
One governance wrinkle is drawing eyebrows: unlike many of his tech peers, Huang is not chairman of Nvidia’s board, according to CNBC.
## Who is Alice Huang, and what is the Megaspeed connection?

Alice Huang, also reported as Huang Le, shows up in coverage as an executive tied to Megaspeed. The House Select Committee on China has labeled her a “publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset.” The New York Times describes a Chinese citizen with polished English and a wide network among senior chip-industry figures, and Bloomberg reports she helped set Megaspeed up. Some outlets call her a former executive. In the reporting reviewed here, she has not publicly responded.

U.S. intelligence reportedly concluded that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her to collect information on Huang, and the Times says Trump administration policymakers received a memo on the subject last spring. Singapore’s government, for its part, says it has not looked into her alleged intelligence ties or her relationship with Huang.
### Megaspeed and the AI chip export-control question
Megaspeed was already on Washington’s radar long before the personal drama surfaced. Here is the tangled backstory:

- **The purchases.** Trade records cited in reports show a Megaspeed-linked Malaysian unit buying at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia technology between June 2024 and February 2026. Senator Tom Cotton and Representative Bill Huizenga cited more than $4.6 billion in an earlier letter.
- **The inspection.** U.S. officials reportedly found Nvidia equipment still sitting in boxes at a Malaysian data center, and the Commerce Department has reportedly been looking into Megaspeed.
- **The worry.** Lawmakers want to know whether chips reached Chinese customers in violation of U.S. export controls. Running chips remotely from outside China is a separate matter and not necessarily illegal.
- **The pushback.** Megaspeed says inspections by the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, Malaysia’s trade ministry and Nvidia found no evidence of illicit transfers. Nvidia says its own checks found Megaspeed legally qualified, with no signs of diversion, and denies any role in smuggling. The reporting does not accuse Nvidia itself of breaking export rules.
To be clear, neither the Commerce probe nor Singapore’s inquiry has publicly established that Megaspeed illegally diverted chips to China.
## Wall Street reaction and Nvidia stock impact

Nvidia shares slipped roughly 4% to 6% in premarket trading Monday, depending on the outlet and the minute. Yahoo Finance reported a 5.5% dip and called it the stock’s lowest level in seven months. At a 5% drop, Bloomberg put the damage near $225 billion in market value.

Two caveats before anyone panics or pounces. First, some of the slide predates the scandal: 24/7 Wall St. notes the stock fell 9.26% last Thursday for reasons unrelated to Huang, so Monday blends sector jitters with leadership worries. Second, not everyone fell. Taiwan’s stock index climbed 4.9%, TSMC gained 4.7%, and AMD reportedly rose about 4% while Nvidia sank.
### The key-person risk

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives called the episode a “black eye” for Huang and framed the investor question bluntly: will he remain CEO? Ives expects Huang to stay on without interruption for now, but concedes there is real risk of removal depending on what the board uncovers. Huang himself owns about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, roughly 3.58% of the company, per its 2026 proxy statement.

History offers a loose compass at best. A 2018 study in the Journal of Financial Economics found stocks fell about 4% on average when the CEO was the one caught, as Yahoo Finance noted. But Nvidia dwarfs every company in that sample, so treat the precedent as a rough guide, not a forecast.
### Congress moves in

The political heat is rising, too. Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Huang for a joint closed-door briefing on November 18, while Democratic lawmakers separately want an investigation or testimony. CNBC reports Democrats are likely to press on whether the administration knew about the relationship and whether Huang swayed American policy, a question raised by Sam Bresnick of Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
## Industry and political reactions: leadership versus national security
Early reactions split along a familiar fault line: Huang’s value to Nvidia on one side, the security questions around him on the other.

- **The White House.** President Trump called Huang a “fine person.” Asked whether he should remain CEO, he said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure,” while noting he had not spoken with Huang about it.
- **The industry.** Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy argued that Huang’s concentrated power is why Nvidia moves faster than anyone, a strength that turns thorny when the person holding it is under review. One investor close to Huang told CNBC that, depending on the findings, a leave of absence is conceivable.
- **The China hawks.** Lawmakers pushing for tighter chip controls, including the Chip Security Act, which would require location checks on export-controlled AI chips, are likely to read the episode as ammunition.
Resolving that tension will not be quick. Huang is simultaneously Nvidia’s strategic engine and, in the current reporting, the figure at the heart of an alleged intelligence operation.
## What investors and Nvidia should expect next

The nearest landmark is November 18, the requested closed-door congressional briefing. After that, the road gets foggy: the board’s investigation has no announced deadline, so uncertainty is the base case, not the exception.
Keep an eye on four things:

1. **How far the board looks.** Whether it stays on the relationship or widens to Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed.
2. **Export-control enforcement.** Any Commerce Department move on Megaspeed, or traction for chip location-verification legislation.
3. **Governance shake-ups.** Any change to Huang’s role, an interim arrangement, or a push to split the chairman and CEO jobs.
4. **Customer and partner mood.** Whether big buyers and Asian suppliers keep seeing this as a leadership story rather than a supply story.

Nvidia’s products and balance sheet are not what the board is examining. Its founder is, and the market is now pricing a risk it has never carried. Be wary of knee-jerk price swings while the facts, especially the intelligence claims, are still being pieced together. This article is news analysis, not investment advice.
## Sources
Figures reflect reporting as of November 9, 2026, and may change.

title: Joo Chiat gets a Shibuya-style scramble crossing, and it starts on 16 November
dek: For three months, people at the East Coast Road and Joo Chiat Road junction will be able to cross diagonally while all traffic stops. Singapore has tried this twice before on Orchard Road.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: Tokyo’s Shibuya scramble crossing at night, the best-known example of the design.
body: Singapore is about to get a little bit of Tokyo. From 16 November, the busy junction of Joo Chiat Road and East Coast Road, outside i12 Katong, will trial a scramble crossing: every vehicle stops at the same time, and people can walk across in any direction, including diagonally.

Marine Parade-Braddell Heights MP Goh Pei Ming told CNA on 11 November that the trial will run for three months. He said it is “part of ongoing efforts to improve traffic flow and enhance pedestrian safety.” The Land Transport Authority (LTA) will watch how traffic and pedestrians cope before deciding whether to keep it.
## The story at a glance

- **Where:** the junction of Joo Chiat Road and East Coast Road, in Katong.
- **When:** from 16 November, for three months.
- **What changes for drivers:** the right turn from East Coast Road into Joo Chiat Road will be permanently restricted.
- **The trade-off:** LTA says waiting times may get longer for both drivers and pedestrians.
## How a scramble crossing works

At a normal junction, people cross alongside the traffic that is moving parallel to them. At a scramble crossing, the lights stop vehicles in every direction for a short time, and the whole junction belongs to pedestrians. Instead of crossing twice to reach the opposite corner, you walk straight across.
The most famous one is Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo, where crowds pour across from every corner at once. That picture is why the Katong trial spread so quickly online this week.
## Not Singapore’s first try

Singapore has tested the idea on Orchard Road before. A scramble crossing ran at the Bideford Road junction for six months from December 2006, and another ran at Cairnhill Road for a month in December 2017. Both were temporary and neither was kept. Malay Mail reported that the country’s only current scramble crossing is in the CBD, near Lau Pa Sat, at Robinson Road and Boon Tat Street.
## What to expect if you go

LTA has been open about the downside: with every vehicle held at once, each light cycle has to make room for a pedestrian-only phase, so drivers and people on foot may wait longer. In return, crossing to the far corner should be quicker and safer, because nobody is turning across your path while you walk.
Drivers heading along East Coast Road who usually turn right into Joo Chiat Road will need another route, because that turn is being restricted for good, not only during the trial.
## Sources

title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after 33 years; CFO Colette Kress takes over for now
dek: Five days after Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into its founder, Huang quit as chief executive and director. The company gave no reason, and its shares fell sharply.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: An Nvidia GeForce RTX graphics card.
body: Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and ran it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday (12 November, US time) as president, chief executive and a member of the board, effective immediately. Nvidia’s announcement did not give a reason.

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer since September 2013, will serve as interim CEO and keep her finance job until a permanent successor is named. The board says it will consider candidates from inside and outside the company. It also appointed Harvey Jones, a director since 1993 and a former chief executive of Synopsys, as its first-ever chair.
## The story at a glance

- **Who leaves:** Jensen Huang, as CEO, president and director, effective immediately.
- **Who steps in:** CFO Colette Kress, as interim CEO.
- **New role:** Harvey Jones becomes the board’s first chair.
- **Reason given:** none.
- **Next date to watch:** Nvidia’s quarterly results, still due on 17 November in the US.
## Five days that shook the world’s biggest chipmaker

On Sunday (8 November), Huang told employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, and apologised to his family and staff. The same day, the board opened an independent investigation into reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. It said it had no reason to believe that national security or Nvidia’s secrets had been compromised. (We covered that day in our report of 9 November.)

On Wednesday, Reuters reported that the board was meeting to consider removing him, and The New York Times reported that his relationship had been with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. On Thursday, he was gone.
Al Jazeera noted that there is no established evidence that Huang knowingly helped Beijing. US lawmakers are examining the national security questions the reports raised.
## What the company said

Nvidia’s statement thanked Huang for his contributions and focused on continuity. “The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team,” Jones said, adding that he expected operations, customer commitments and the product road map to continue without interruption. Kress said her focus was on serving the company’s customers, partners, developers and shareholders.
## How the market took it

Nvidia’s shares fell sharply on Thursday. Al Jazeera reported they were down by more than 14% at one point before recovering some ground. Huang owns about 3.6% of the company, a stake Fortune valued at about US$150 billion.
## Who could run Nvidia next?

Reuters has listed possible candidates, including Kress, Nvidia executive Ian Buck, Arm chief executive Rene Haas and AMD chief executive Lisa Su. US President Donald Trump, who defended Huang throughout the week, suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook. There is no sign that Cook is interested.
## What happens next

Nvidia says it will report its third-quarter results on Tuesday, 17 November, as previously scheduled, at about 1.20 p.m. Pacific time. That is early on Wednesday, 18 November, in Singapore. Investors will be listening for two things: whether the company’s growth forecast holds, and what Kress says about the search for a permanent leader.

title: Microsoft says it is “deeply sorry” after a global Outlook outage spanned two working days
dek: Millions of people couldn’t reach their email from early Friday, Singapore time. Microsoft blamed a hidden fault from a network upgrade, and said it was not a hack.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: A Microsoft Surface laptop.
body: **Update, 14 November:** Microsoft has apologised and given a cause. The story below has been updated.

If your work email went quiet on Friday, you weren’t alone. Microsoft’s Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services went down around the world, leaving businesses, schools, hospitals and government offices unable to send or read mail. For some users, the trouble ran from Thursday into Friday in the US, across two full working days.

Microsoft first said it was investigating reports of people being unable to reach their mailboxes shortly before 1 p.m. US Eastern time on Thursday, 12 November. That was just before 2 a.m. on Friday in Singapore. Within an hour of that first post, Downdetector had logged more than 100,000 reports, ABC News said.
## The story at a glance

- **What broke:** access to Outlook mailboxes, with problems also reported in Teams and other Microsoft 365 apps.
- **Where:** at first the Americas; Microsoft later said users in any region could be affected.
- **Cause:** a fault left by an earlier network capacity upgrade, exposed by a recent network change.
- **Not a hack:** Microsoft said there was no sign of malicious or cyber activity.
- **Apology:** issued about 24 hours after the outage began.
## What went wrong

Microsoft’s early updates pointed to problems with server availability. Its fuller explanation came on Friday: an issue introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade had stayed hidden until a more recent network change brought it to the surface.

“This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents,” the company said. To stop the damage, Microsoft paused deployments, moved traffic away from the affected infrastructure and restarted servers. Teams was restored first. By Friday morning in the US, Microsoft said email queues were approaching normal levels, though some people could still see delays or patchy access.
## The apology

“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” Microsoft said on Friday, adding that it takes the trust customers place in it extremely seriously. Charles Lamanna, an executive vice-president at the company, had already said late on Thursday: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers.”
Variety reported that affected business customers can ask Microsoft for service credits.

The outage reached well beyond offices. New York City’s emergency management agency warned that people might struggle to reach city departments, and told residents to call 311 for non-emergencies and 911 in an emergency.
## If your business runs on one email provider
This part is our advice, not Microsoft’s. Outages like this are rare, but when they happen, everything that depends on one service stops at once.

- **Keep a second way to reach your team,** such as a phone tree or a group chat on another service.
- **Bookmark the provider’s status page,** so you can tell a global outage from a problem on your side.
- **Don’t panic-reset passwords or reinstall apps** during a confirmed outage. It rarely helps and can lock you out later.
- **If you pay for business plans,** check your service agreement for credits after a long outage.
## Sources

title: SpaceX catches a Starship upper stage with its launch tower for the first time
dek: After 14 trips around Earth, the ship settled into the tower’s giant arms in Texas. The booster wasn’t so lucky: it aborted its own catch and exploded over the Gulf of Mexico.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: SpaceX’s Starbase launch site, with rockets and cranes.
body: SpaceX has done something no one had done before: brought the top half of a rocket back from orbit and caught it in mid-air. On Saturday (14 November, US time), the upper stage of Starship, known simply as “the ship”, descended into the mechanical arms of its launch tower at Starbase in South Texas.
“Mechazilla catches Starship!” the company posted. Videos of the catch spread across social media within minutes.
## The story at a glance

- **Flight:** Starship’s 15th test flight, launched on Friday, 13 November, from Starbase in Texas.
- **In orbit:** about 22 hours and 14 trips around Earth, deploying 26 Starlink V3 internet satellites.
- **The catch:** the ship was caught by the tower’s arms on Saturday, 14 November, a first.
- **The miss:** the Super Heavy booster called off its own catch, diverted towards the Gulf of Mexico and exploded.
## Why catching the ship matters

SpaceX has caught its huge Super Heavy boosters with the same tower arms before. The ship is a much harder problem: it comes back from orbit at enormous speed and has to survive re-entry before slowing down enough to be caught. Until now, ships ended their flights with a splashdown or worse.

Catching the ship intact is the step that could make the whole rocket reusable, like an aircraft that flies, lands and flies again. That is the idea behind SpaceX’s promise of much cheaper trips to orbit, and it matters for NASA too: the agency is paying SpaceX to build a version of Starship to land astronauts on the Moon, with a crewed landing planned for 2028.
## The booster that didn’t make it

The flight had aimed for a first-ever double catch, with the booster caught soon after launch and the ship a day later. Instead, the booster’s guidance system spotted a problem on the way back and automatically cancelled the catch. It turned away towards the Gulf of Mexico and exploded before reaching the water.

“It was doing what it was supposed to do,” SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot told UPI, explaining that the system detected the booster was not where it needed to be for a catch. Steering a failing rocket away from the tower protects the tower, which SpaceX needs for the next flight.
## What’s next

Elon Musk has said he wants Starship to fly weekly, and eventually twice a week, as SpaceX works towards fast reuse. The next obvious milestone is the one this flight missed: catching both halves of the same rocket.

title: Jensen Huang’s next move: exile, comeback, or something else?
dek: Three days after resigning as Nvidia’s chief executive, Huang was reportedly discussing a return with allies. Here is what we know, what is only reported, and what stands in the way.
author: TNS Newsroom
caption: The Nvidia logo.
body: **Update, 18 November:** The comeback hit a wall. On Nvidia’s results call on 17 November (US time), board chair Harvey Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate” Huang as CEO, and that it has hired the search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent leader. Huang had posted earlier that day that he would be “honored” to return if the board thought it was in the company’s interest. The results themselves were strong: third-quarter revenue of US$115.8 billion, up 103% on a year earlier, and a forecast of about US$130 billion for the current quarter. More in the section at the end. The story below was published on 16 November.
Can you resign on a Thursday and be talking about a comeback by Sunday? Jensen Huang seems to be trying.

On Sunday (15 November), the Financial Times reported that Huang was considering a return as Nvidia’s chief executive and had discussed the idea with confidants, just three days after he resigned. One ally told the paper they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and win support from the White House. Neither Huang nor Nvidia has confirmed any of it.
## The story at a glance

- **What happened:** Huang resigned as Nvidia’s president, CEO and director on 12 November. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
- **What’s reported:** Huang is discussing a comeback with allies (Financial Times, 15 November).
- **The biggest hurdle:** the board’s independent investigation, and scrutiny in Washington over chip sales to China.
- **The next clue:** Nvidia’s results on 17 November (early on 18 November in Singapore), and what the board says about leadership.
## What we know, and what is only reported
This story has moved fast, so it helps to separate the facts from the reporting.

- **Fact: the resignation.** Nvidia announced on 12 November that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. It gave no reason.
- **Fact: the investigation.** The board opened an independent investigation on 8 November into reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to look into his conduct, CNBC reported.
- **Fact: the stand-in.** Colette Kress, CFO for 13 years, is interim CEO. The board says it will look at candidates from inside and outside the company.
- **Fact: the market.** Nvidia shares fell 13% in the week to 13 November, their worst week since April 2025 and their sixth weekly fall in a row, the longest streak since 2012, CNBC reported. The stock is roughly a third below its record close of early October.
- **Reported, not confirmed: the comeback.** It comes from the Financial Times’ sources. CNBC, citing a person familiar with the matter, reported on 16 November that the board is not considering bringing Huang back.
## How would a comeback even work?
Not easily. The board would first need to finish its investigation, or at least narrow it, and it would have to do that with regulators and lawmakers watching closely.

The pressure runs in both directions. Two big shareholders, Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management, wrote to the board on 13 November asking for a “slow, measured, and deliberate” leadership process that keeps “the potential return of Jensen Huang” on the table. They did not ask for him to be reinstated straight away. Elon Musk said he had signed a petition calling for Huang’s return, and US President Donald Trump said on 16 November that he would not mind seeing it.

Washington is pulling the other way. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly blamed the Commerce Department for being slow to restrict exports to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the centre of the spy reports, and lawmakers from both parties have pressed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.
## Why customers and investors care

Nvidia sells the chips that most of the world’s AI is trained on, and many of its biggest customers sign long, complex supply deals. Musk argued that without Huang, “critical deals will be lost”. Kress’s job is to prove him wrong by showing customers that nothing changes on their side.

- **Cloud buyers** will want proof of continuity: the same road map, the same delivery dates.
- **Investors** are pricing a risk they have never had to think about: Nvidia without its founder.
- **Succession** is wide open. Reuters has listed AMD’s Lisa Su among possible outside candidates, and the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm’s Rene Haas.
## Our read

This section is our analysis, and the facts could change quickly. The most likely path is an earnings call that stresses continuity, a long investigation and, eventually, a negotiated outcome. That could mean Huang returning, Huang becoming an adviser, or a clean exit. The biggest risks are political: pressure from Congress, and the long shadow of US–China chip rules. If the board rushed to bring him back, it would invite exactly the scrutiny it is trying to get past.
## After the results: what changed on 17 November

- **The board said no, for now.** Chair Harvey Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate” Huang, would not discuss the circumstances of his resignation, and has full confidence in Kress as interim CEO. The search, run by Heidrick & Struggles, will consider internal and external candidates.
- **Huang said yes, if asked.** In a post on X, he said he would be “honored” to return if the board thought it was in Nvidia’s interest, and that he is cooperating with the investigation. He has agreed to a closed-door interview with the US House of Representatives on 1 December, NBC News reported.
- **The numbers held up.** Revenue was US$115.8 billion in the quarter to 25 October, up 103% on a year earlier and ahead of analysts’ estimates. Data centre revenue was US$107.6 billion. Nvidia forecast about US$130 billion for the current quarter, assuming no data centre chip sales to China. “Our momentum is real,” Kress said.
- **The shares steadied.** Nvidia closed at US$155.46 on 17 November, down 0.4%, then rose about 5% in after-hours trading as the call ended. That still left the stock about 35% below its record close of US$239.24 on 6 October.
